Kevin Lamour has hit out at Gianni Infantino over his plan to sell stakes in the organisation. (Getty Images: Joosep Martinson)

FIFA chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, says FIFA president Gianni Infantino's sell-off idea is the "project of one person".

Mr Lamour all but invited Mr Infantino to sack him over his comments, saying he would "sleep well tonight".

A September 19 deadline has been set for football federations to decide on the proposal.

FIFA's chief operating officer said its staff were deceived by president Gianni Infantino's World Cup sell-off plan, and suggested the project must not go ahead.

Zurich-based executive Kevin Lamour all but invited Infantino to fire him in a statement to the Associated Press that defended his colleagues amid intense fallout from the FIFA boss's plan to sell stakes in future World Cup profits to private equity funds.

Mr Lamour wrote that staff were "deceived" by Mr Infantino's lack of openness in planning the sale over recent months and "deserve better than contempt and intimidation".

"It is the project of one person," wrote Lamour, a long-time colleague of Infantino at both FIFA and European soccer body UEFA.

Gianni Infantino (left) and Donald Trump were often seen together during and in the lead-up to the 2026 World Cup. (Getty Images: Chris Brunskill)

"Not only must this project not go ahead … but the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions."

Mr Lamour's statement came hours after Mr Infantino's senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro, a former Goldman Sachs banker who represented the soccer body on the White House Task Force for the World Cup, resigned and urged other senior FIFA staff to speak out.

"I cannot stand by while FIFA considers selling a stake in the World Cup," Mr Cordeiro wrote in a statement. The former US Soccer Federation president said he was not included in talks about the plan backed by a New York investment fund created by Joshua Kushner.

"Let me be clear. I had no involvement in this proposal, and I oppose it unequivocally," Mr Cordeiro said. He called the $US20 billion ($28.5 billion) commercial subsidiary "a bad deal for football".

Mr Lamour did not resign the post he has held since 2024 but said he had a duty to his colleagues.

Joshua Kushner (right) with brother Jared, is leading the charge to make a private investment in FIFA. (Getty Images: Patrick McMullan)

"And if that means I lose my job then so be it," the French official said.

"I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight."

Mr Lamour came to soccer from politics two decades ago as an aide to then-UEFA president Michel Platini. He often had an international role in soccer politics, liaising with FIFA member federations in Africa and Asia, who are weighing their own decisions on Mr Infantino's offers of $US20 million each by a deadline of September 19.

Mr Cordeiro often joined Mr Infantino on working visits to meet US President Donald Trump at the White House in recent years.

"Football has been central to my life, and after more than 35 years in banking I understand both the value of this asset and the consequences of giving part of it away," he said.

"That is why this proposal should be rejected."

Mr Infantino has proposed spinning off FIFA's commercial businesses — including World Cups and Club World Cups for men and women — into a $20 billion subsidiary with 20 per cent owned by private investors.

The "anchor investor," described by FIFA, is Kushner, the younger brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

"FIFA already has access to extraordinary financial resources. The organisation sits on billions of dollars in reserves and no debt," Mr Cordeiro said. He noted FIFA's revenue of $15 billion in the past four years tied to the men's World Cup just ended.

Gianni Infantino's plan to sell stakes in FIFA's events and competitions arm to investors would grant them control over the World Cup.

"Against that backdrop, selling a permanent stake in football's most valuable asset to raise $4.2 billion makes little sense. It is mortgaging football's future without any compelling justification," he said.

Mr Cordeiro said he shared five years of working for FIFA alongside Infantino with "dedicated, principled people who care deeply about the game".

"I hope they, too, will speak up," he wrote, "because decisions of this magnitude should be made in the interests of football, not those who stand to profit from it."

Mr Infantino has been president of FIFA for more than 10 years and seemed sure to be re-elected unopposed next March. FIFA has set a November 18 deadline for challengers to come forward.

Mr Lamour was part of Mr Infantino's inner circle that campaigned for him to become the surprise winner of that FIFA presidential election in February 2016.
